strengths: Well-motivated extension of probabilistic adversarial attacks to concept-level, with clear intuition via Figure 1
Strong white-box targeted attack success rates (97.82% vs 84.23% for DiffAttack)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation including white-box/black-box attacks on 9 classifiers, multiple image quality metrics, user studies, and sensitivity analyses
Superior concept preservation compared to baselines (user study 0.9654, better CLIP/quality metrics in some cases)
Practical methodology well-documented with extensive implementation details (hyperparameters, appendices, code promised)
Addresses real limitation of single-image perturbations in unrestricted adversarial settings
weaknesses: Limited novelty: straightforward extension of Zhang et al. [49] from single images to concept sets; core probabilistic framework and pipeline unchanged

Weak theoretical contributions: Theorem 1 is basic calculus (KL divergence to Gaussian), Theorem 2 is algebra; restrictive assumptions (identical means, Gaussian distributions) with limited verification
Significant computational cost inadequately addressed: ~8.3 hours per concept (SDXL LoRA 20min + diffusion fine-tuning 8hrs) versus brief dismissal in Section 7; severely limits reproducibility
Limited evaluation scope: only 26 of 30 concepts, only 30 of 1000 ImageNet classes, 780 total examples; generalization unclear

Mixed transferability results: conservative strategy often underperforms baselines (VGG19 20.90% vs DiffAttack 31.41%), suggesting white-box overfitting; aggressive strategy uses different selection criteria confounding comparison
Concept definition remains vague despite claims in Section 8; distinction between concept/class/identity unclear; practical guidance in Section 8 is hand-wavy
Suspicious evaluation metrics: Table 2 shows CLIP similarity *lower* for CONS (0.8283 vs 0.8581), contradicting preservation claims; user study limited (5 annotators)
Sample selection strategy ad-hoc and potentially suboptimal: conservative strategy uses 'lowest softmax probability' (counterintuitive), ranking indirect versus direct objective optimization
Missing ablations: no analysis of minimum concept set size, concept type effectiveness, or SDXL augmentation quality impact
Likelihood estimation noisy (Appendix B Table 3 shows large variance, e.g., ±4447.21) with strong unverified assumptions about p_share; sensitivity not analyzed

strengths: Clear motivation and presentation with effective visualizations (Figure 1) illustrating the core idea of expanding attack distributions from single images to concepts
Comprehensive empirical evaluation including 26 concepts, 30 ImageNet target classes, multiple victim models, user studies, and extensive image quality metrics
Strong empirical results showing improved concept preservation (0.9654 user similarity vs. 0.7577 for DiffAttack) and higher white-box success rates (97.82%)
Practical methodological contributions including concept augmentation strategy using SDXL LoRA and detailed finetuning guidelines
Principled probabilistic framework with Theorem 2 providing tractable KL divergence comparison metrics
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contribution is using |C_ori| > 1 instead of |C_ori| = 1 in Zhang et al. [49], which is a hyperparameter adjustment rather than fundamental innovation. ProbAttack is acknowledged as a special case, making the advance incremental

Vague concept definition despite claims of clarity: Section 8 admits 'the term concept is difficult to define precisely' with no principled guidelines beyond intuitive pose/viewpoint/background variations

Weak theoretical contributions: Theorem 1 is a straightforward calculus result (KL decreases with variance), essentially circular given problem setup. Gaussian distribution assumption for p_dis is never validated empirically on finetuned diffusion models

Questionable stability of empirical estimates: Table 3 shows huge standard deviations in ΔK L estimates (often comparable to or exceeding the means, e.g., ±2040.85), raising concerns about reliability. No analysis of why estimates are so noisy or implications for theoretical framework

Computational overhead makes practical applicability questionable: requires ~20 min SDXL + ~8 hours diffusion finetuning per concept. Dismissal that 'one successful example causes damage' ignores realistic scenarios requiring multiple concepts. Unfair comparison with orders-of-magnitude-faster baselines

Transferability trade-offs inadequately explored: aggressive strategy achieves better transferability by selecting higher target probability examples (may not transfer robustly), while conservative strategy merely matches baselines. Table 4 shows increasing M with |C_ori|=30 *decreases* transferability, suggesting overfitting to white-box classifier
Limited experimental scope: only 26 concepts (4 excluded), 30 ImageNet target classes; no untargeted attacks; only diffusion-based p_dis; no evaluation on other datasets; generalization unclear

Concept augmentation is not methodologically novel: entirely relies on existing tools (SDXL LoRA + GPT-4o) without principled contribution; specific prompts appear arbitrary and are not systematically analyzed
Sample selection strategy (conservative vs. aggressive) crucial for performance but lacks principled justification. Why rank by target probability then use these specific tie-breaking criteria?

Insufficient exploration of what makes good concept datasets: the critical trade-off between concept diversity and discrimination difficulty (noted in Section 8) is not systematically studied across different concept types

strengths: Novel concept-based attack framework that intuitively extends adversarial attacks from single images to entire concepts, with strong motivation (Figure 1) and clear practical implications

Comprehensive experimental evaluation at scale (26 concepts × 30 classes = 780 examples) across multiple dimensions: white-box success, black-box transferability, concept preservation via user study, and 7 image quality metrics

Strong empirical results demonstrating clear improvements: 97.82% white-box success vs 84.23% (DiffAttack), user study scores of 0.9654 vs 0.8041 (ProbAttack), superior image quality across all metrics
Solid theoretical framework with formal proofs of Theorems 1 and 2 providing justification for variance expansion and tractable KL divergence estimation
Practical methodology with clear concept augmentation strategy (SDXL LoRA + GPT-4o), well-designed sample selection strategies (conservative/aggressive), and useful ablation studies
Excellent presentation with clear writing, informative figures, and comprehensive appendices; detailed reproducibility information including hyperparameters and promised code release

Evaluation across diverse architectures (VGG, ResNet, DenseNet, Inception, EfficientNet) and defense-trained models; additional experiments with different surrogate models (MobileNetV2, ViT-Base) provided
weaknesses: Theoretical contributions are relatively limited: Theorem 1 is a straightforward KL divergence derivative, Theorem 2 is essentially a KL definition rearrangement; connection between variance and practical attack success not rigorously established; Gaussian distribution assumption may not hold but not discussed

Significant computational overhead inadequately addressed: 8 hours diffusion finetuning per concept (208 hours total for 26 concepts on H100 GPU), but cost-vs-performance trade-off not quantitatively compared to single-image baselines; fairness of comparison with M=10 samples unclear

Evaluation scope limitations: only 30/1000 ImageNet classes, 26/30 DreamBooth concepts usable (4 excluded), evaluation limited to object identity concepts; unclear generalization to other concept types (scenes, abstract concepts, semantic categories); no evaluation on standard robustness benchmarks

Sample selection strategies appear somewhat ad-hoc: limited justification for conservative/aggressive criteria based on softmax probability; Table 4 reveals concerning trade-off where transferability decreases with larger M when |Cori|=30, suggesting fundamental tension between concept preservation and attack effectiveness

Limited novelty over prior work: core mathematical framework directly from Zhang et al. [49]; extension to concepts is meaningful but incremental; relationship to Song et al. [38] class-level attacks could be more clearly distinguished

Incomplete practical applicability analysis: requires diverse image sets or generative capability, fine-tuning of both generative and diffusion models (~28 hours total per concept), likely impractical for novel concepts; complexity far exceeds single-image attacks

Concept preservation evaluation limited: user study on final selected examples only (selection bias), CLIP similarity drops to 0.8283 (AGGR), no analysis of which perturbation types (pose vs. color vs. background) cause misclassification

Missing key ablations: no systematic analysis of concept diversity vs. success, no investigation of which concepts are harder to attack and why, limited discussion of why 4 concepts couldn't be augmented, no analysis of within-concept distance effects

Ethical concerns mentioned but not thoroughly addressed: potential for misuse in identification acknowledged but no countermeasures discussed; increased detectability challenges compared to imperceptible perturbations not analyzed

Experimental fairness concerns: other unrestricted attack methods (ACA, DiffAttack) might benefit from similar sampling strategies; whether different computational budgets are fairly compared not clearly stated

strengths: Novel concept-level adversarial attack framework with clear theoretical motivation; principled extension of probabilistic adversarial attacks from single images to concept distributions
Strong white-box attack results: 97.82% top-1 success on ResNet50 with superior concept preservation (0.9654 user study similarity vs. 0.8041 for ProbAttack)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple surrogate classifiers, 9 transfer targets, and extensive metrics (user study + 7 image quality measures) across 780 adversarial examples
Solid theoretical foundation with rigorous proofs (Theorems 1-2) and empirical validation showing Δ < 0 for all 26 concepts, supporting theoretical predictions
Practical concept augmentation strategy using LoRA + GPT-4 prompting to expand limited concept datasets; demonstrates accessibility
Excellent reproducibility with code availability, complete hyperparameters, detailed proofs, user study methodology, and compute resource specifications
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core contribution (replacing x_ori with C_ori in equation 2→3) is straightforward and incremental over Zhang et al. (2024b), as acknowledged by authors

Black-box transferability remains weak (2.05% top-5 on VGG19 vs. 2.44% for ProbAttack), severely limiting practical threat value; Appendix H admits achieving high transferability would require compromising identity preservation
Prohibitive computational cost: 8 hours fine-tuning per concept (24× slower than ProbAttack), requiring H100 GPUs; severely limits reproducibility and practical deployment applicability
Narrow evaluation scope: only 26 concepts evaluated (4 DreamBooth excluded), 30/1000 ImageNet classes, exclusively concrete objects; no evaluation on non-ImageNet domains or abstract concepts

Theory-practice gaps: Theorem 1 assumes Gibbs distributions not guaranteed by practical diffusion models; condition E[D(X,μ)]>E_q[D(X,μ)] assumed but unverified; Appendix B's pshare assumption validity unvalidated
High unexplained variance in Table 4: Δ ranges from -219 to -12401 across concepts with no analysis of causes or correlations with attack success

Concept specification challenges: no principled guidance on |C_ori| size/diversity requirements; concept augmentation success depends on SDXL robustness; Appendix K acknowledges infeasibility under practical constraints
Ad-hoc sample selection: conservative vs. aggressive strategies lack principled framework; Appendix C shows conservative strategy counterintuitively decreases transferability with larger |C_ori|
Incomplete ablation studies: limited sensitivity analysis; missing investigation of which concept types benefit most; no analysis of augmentation quality sensitivity

Ethical concerns inadequately addressed: potential for selling prohibited items and adversarial patch attacks acknowledged but proposed defenses (adversarial training, AI-generated content detection) are generic and potentially insufficient

strengths: Clear problem motivation with effective visualization (Figure 1) of concept-based vs. single-image adversarial attacks
Solid theoretical contributions with two formal theorems providing mathematical justification for the approach, including practical KL divergence estimation techniques
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple victim classifiers, user study validating concept preservation (0.96+ similarity), and extensive image quality metrics
Strong white-box attack performance (97.82% Top-1 success rate on ResNet50)
Practical implementation details using modern generative models (SDXL LoRA + GPT-4o) for concept augmentation
Commitment to reproducibility with promised code release and detailed hyperparameter specifications
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: the essential contribution is replacing x_ori with C_ori (concept distribution) in Zhang et al. (2024b)'s framework—operationally straightforward without substantial conceptual advance
Critical transferability failure: black-box Top-5 success (2.05-4.36%) shows essentially no improvement over baselines (ProbAttack: 2.44%), which is the most important metric for adversarial attacks
Prohibitive computational cost: 8 hours per concept fine-tuning vs. 20 minutes for ProbAttack severely limits scalability and practical applicability; only 3-4 attacks per day per concept
Vague concept definition: paper acknowledges difficulty in defining concepts precisely; two instantiation approaches lack principled guidance; no clear criteria for what constitutes 'same concept'
Narrow evaluation scope: only 26/30 concepts (4 excluded), 30/1000 ImageNet classes, no evaluation on diverse domains (faces, scenes, abstract objects); unclear scalability
Theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 assumes Gibbs distribution but doesn't prove diffusion models satisfy this; Theorem 2 provides formula but not actionable insights into when concept-based approach wins
Weak experimental baselines: limited comparison to other unrestricted attacks; concept/class-based methods (Song et al. 2018, Collins et al. 2025) only compared in capability matrix, not performance
Soft evaluation metrics: user study with only 5 annotators (no inter-annotator agreement reported); CLIP similarity and image quality metrics are proxies rather than direct measures
Limited practical applicability: method requires extensive concept datasets, but many realistic scenarios involve single/few images; augmentation requires expensive commercial APIs
Presentation: 34-page paper with important limitations in appendices; overstated claims ('herald the future of adversarial attacks'); concept vs. class distinction unclear early on

strengths: Clear and well-motivated conceptual contribution extending single-image to concept-based attacks with effective visualization
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple baselines, victim classifiers, and metrics with 780 adversarial examples
Strong white-box attack success rates (97.82% top-1 on ResNet50) with excellent concept preservation (0.9654 user study similarity)
Practical and reproducible augmentation pipeline using SDXL, LoRA, and GPT-4o for concept diversity
Excellent presentation, detailed proofs, hyperparameters, and reproducibility materials promised
Thoughtful ethics discussion with mitigation strategies and broader impact analysis
Empirical validation of KL divergence reduction hypothesis across all 26 concepts
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: straightforward parameter substitution (xori→Cori) in existing framework, not a fundamentally new principle
Weak theoretical contributions: Theorems 1-2 are standard mathematical results that don't explain why expanded distributions yield better attacks
Poor black-box transferability (2-11% top-5) severely limits practical applicability despite strong white-box performance
Significant computational overhead: 8 hours fine-tuning per concept (24× slower than ProbAttack) without principled justification
Missing critical ablation: effect of augmented dataset alone on ProbAttack baseline not evaluated, unclear where improvements originate
Limited experimental scope: only 26 DreamBooth objects and 30 ImageNet classes; no evaluation on other domains
Concept dataset requirement adds complexity; augmentation depends on SDXL quality; applicability limited to object-centric scenarios
User study limited to 5 annotators on ResNet50 only; concept preservation claims partially subjective
